name: Ice mass

source.name: IMBIE 2026 (UK Polar Data Centre)
source.citation: Otosaka, I., Shepherd, A., Amory, C., et al. (2026). Mass balance of the Greenland and Antarctic Ice Sheets from the 1970s to 2023 (Version 1.0) [Data set]. NERC EDS UK Polar Data Centre. https://doi.org/10.5285/128c5e33-5224-4197-82f0-19dcc95b80a0
processing: Downloaded the per-region CSV files (imbie3_<region>_Gt_partitioned.csv) unchanged.
Used the total cumulative mass balance column and its 1-sigma uncertainty, monthly, as published.
No smoothing, gap filling or extrapolation.

describe.what: How much ice an ice sheet holds, compared with the start of its record.
describe.whyItMatters: Ice lost from the ice sheets raises sea level; about 362 Gt is 1 mm.

notes: Record starts in July 1971 for Greenland and 1979 for Antarctica.
Uncertainty (1-sigma) is larger early in the record.
Cumulative mass is relative to the start of the record, not the total mass of the ice sheet.
Reconciled from many satellite surveys (gravity, altimetry and the input-output method), not one instrument.
Before 1992 the record rests on fewer, older methods, so the uncertainty is larger early.
Not independent of GRACE-based ice maps or sea-level budgets: gravimetry is one of IMBIE's methods.

name: Ice mass change rate

source.name: IMBIE 2026 (UK Polar Data Centre)
source.citation: Otosaka, I., Shepherd, A., Amory, C., et al. (2026). Mass balance of the Greenland and Antarctic Ice Sheets from the 1970s to 2023 (Version 1.0) [Data set]. NERC EDS UK Polar Data Centre. https://doi.org/10.5285/128c5e33-5224-4197-82f0-19dcc95b80a0
processing: Downloaded the per-region CSV files (imbie3_<region>_Gt_partitioned.csv) unchanged.
Annual rate = mean of the 12 published monthly rate rows of each calendar year; years with fewer than 12 months are left out (no padding).
Never recomputed by differencing the cumulative series.

describe.what: How fast an ice sheet gains or loses ice each year.
describe.whyItMatters: A trend in the rate means the loss is speeding up or slowing down.

notes: A trend in this series is an acceleration (Gt/yr per year).
Published rates change about once a year, so each calendar year is one point.
Reconciled from many satellite surveys (gravity, altimetry and the input-output method), not one instrument.
Before 1992 the record rests on fewer, older methods, so the uncertainty is larger early.
Not independent of GRACE-based ice maps or sea-level budgets: gravimetry is one of IMBIE's methods.

name: Ice Extent

source.name: ITS_LIVE Greenland ice sheet extent masks, NSIDC-0793 v1
source.citation: Greene, C. A., Gardner, A. S., Wood, M. & Cuzzone, J. K. (2024). MEaSUREs ITS_LIVE Greenland Monthly 120 m Ice Sheet Extent Masks, 1972-2022 (NSIDC-0793, Version 1). Boulder, Colorado USA: NASA NSIDC DAAC. https://doi.org/10.5067/579TO87M7IZB
source.licence: NASA open data (NSIDC use and copyright guidelines)
processing: Downloaded the 120 m monthly ice mask unchanged (the MP4 animations were not used).
Monthly ice area = number of ice pixels x 0.0144 km2, corrected for the polar-stereographic map scale (spherical formula).
Months without terminus observations are gap-filled by the source, not by us.
Globe outlines: yearly mean cover on a 4.8 km grid, contoured at 50%, simplified to 3 km (display only).

describe.what: The area of Greenland covered by ice, month by month.
describe.whyItMatters: Retreating glacier fronts shrink the ice-covered area.

notes: Greenland only.
Early years have more missing months (sparse imagery).
Outlines are coarse; the record is computed from 120 m masks we do not ship.
Derived from glacier terminus positions; interior ice is fixed, so the change is at the glacier fronts.
Months without terminus observations are gap-filled by the source, so neighbouring months are not independent.
An area is not a mass: a retreating front does not equal mass loss (ice mass is a separate variable).

name: Summer air temperature

source.name: NASA MERRA-2 monthly 2 m air temperature (M2TMNXSLV v5.12.4, GES DISC)
source.citation: Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) (2015), MERRA-2 tavgM_2d_slv_Nx: 2d, Monthly mean, Time-Averaged, Single-Level, Assimilation, Single-Level Diagnostics V5.12.4, Greenbelt, MD, USA, Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center (GES DISC), doi:10.5067/AP1B0BA5PD2K
source.licence: NASA open data (GES DISC data use guidelines)
processing: Downloaded only the T2M field of each monthly file through NASA's OPeNDAP service (values unchanged).
Region mean = area-weighted mean of the 0.5 x 0.625 degree cells whose centre lies inside the region outline.
Summer = June-August for northern regions (Greenland, Himalayas); December-February for Antarctica, labelled by the year of its January; only summers with all three months.
Shown as the difference from the 1991-2020 average summer (kelvin differences = degrees C).
Map: each month minus the 1991-2020 mean of that calendar month, interpolated to a 1-degree grid.

describe.what: Summer air temperature near the surface, as a difference from the 1991-2020 average.
describe.whyItMatters: Warm summers drive surface melt on Greenland.

notes: Greenland: June-August mean. Antarctica: December-February mean, labelled by the year of its January.
Anomaly from the 1991-2020 average.
Reanalysis, not direct measurement. Greenland summers from 1980, Antarctic summers from 1981 (the first full December-February in MERRA-2).
Reanalysis: a NASA weather model constrained by observations, not a direct measurement; over the ice sheet interiors, where observations are sparse, values lean on the model.
2 m air temperature of a model grid cell (about 50 km), not a station value.

name: Sea level

source.name: NASA-SSH simple gridded sea surface height V1.1 (PO.DAAC)
source.citation: Willis, J. (2026). NASA-SSH Simple Gridded Sea Surface Height from Standardized Reference Missions Only Version 1.1. PO.DAAC. https://doi.org/10.5067/NSREF-SG0V11. Area means over our polygons by Trend Detective.
processing: Downloaded the weekly 0.5-degree grids unchanged.
Area-weighted mean of the valid cells inside each sea's polygon (polygons kept about 100 km offshore); the global mean uses all valid cells.
Monthly value = mean of the weeks labelled in that month (at least 3 weeks, else missing).
No glacial isostatic adjustment, no land subsidence, no gap filling or extrapolation.

describe.what: Sea level measured by satellites since 1993: the global mean, or the mean over one coastal sea.
describe.whyItMatters: Rising seas threaten coasts worldwide, and some seas rise faster than the global mean.

notes: Global: the mean over the whole ocean, not the value at any place.
Coastal seas: the mean over the sea area drawn on the globe, not the value at a town or harbour, and not the rise people feel on land.
Land subsidence is not included. Where the land sinks, the local rise is larger than shown.
Satellite (absolute) sea level. Satellite data are less reliable near land, so each coastal-sea area keeps about 100 km away from the coast: it describes the open sea, not the shore.
Coastal seas swing more from year to year (El Nino, monsoon, winds) than the global mean, so a trend there needs a longer record to stand out.
Each coastal sea has its own notes, shown when it is selected.
Global series not corrected for glacial isostatic adjustment.
No per-point uncertainty in the source.

name: Sea level, long record

source.name: JPL_RECON_GMSL v1.0 (PO.DAAC; Frederikse et al. 2020)
source.citation: Frederikse, T., Landerer, F., Caron, L., et al. (2020). The causes of sea-level rise since 1900. Nature 584, 393-397, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2591-3. Data: JPL_RECON_GMSL v1.0, PO.DAAC, https://doi.org/10.5067/GMSLT-FJPL1
processing: Downloaded global_timeseries_measures.nc unchanged.
Used global_average_sea_level_change and its 5-95% lower and upper bounds, annual, as published.
No smoothing, gap filling or extrapolation; never joined to the satellite record.

describe.what: Global mean sea level since 1900, reconstructed from tide gauges and models.
describe.whyItMatters: Shows how fast sea level rose before satellites.

notes: Separate from the satellite record; never joined to it.
Global only.
Bounds are 5-95%.
Reconstructed from tide gauges, corrected for land motion, plus models; not satellite data.
Global mean only; it is not the sea level at any place.
Ends in 2018; the satellite record (1993 onward) is a separate variable and is never joined to it.

name: Ice mass, long record

source.name: JPL_RECON_GMSL v1.0 (PO.DAAC; Frederikse et al. 2020)
source.citation: Frederikse, T., Landerer, F., Caron, L., et al. (2020). The causes of sea-level rise since 1900. Nature 584, 393-397, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2591-3. Data: JPL_RECON_GMSL v1.0, PO.DAAC, https://doi.org/10.5067/GMSLT-FJPL1
processing: Downloaded global_timeseries_measures.nc unchanged.
Used the Greenland (GrIS) and Antarctic (AIS) sea-level contributions and their 5-95% bounds.
Converted mm of sea level to ice mass change in Gt with 362 Gt = 1 mm, sign flipped so ice loss is negative mass (as in IMBIE).
No smoothing, gap filling or extrapolation; never joined to the IMBIE record.

describe.what: Ice sheet mass change since 1900, reconstructed.
describe.whyItMatters: Puts the satellite era in a longer context.

notes: Separate from the IMBIE record; never joined to it.
Greenland includes peripheral glaciers. Before 2003 (before gravity satellites) it rests on reconstructions from models, older images and field data.
Bounds are 5-95%.
Before the satellite era the values come from reconstructions with large uncertainty (see the bounds).
Not independent of IMBIE and GRACE in the recent decades: the reconstruction uses them.

name: Monsoon rainfall

source.name: NASA GPM IMERG Final monthly precipitation V07 (GPM_3IMERGM, GES DISC)
source.citation: Huffman, G.J., Stocker, E.F., Bolvin, D.T., Nelkin, E.J., Tan, J. (2023), GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 1 month 0.1 degree x 0.1 degree V07, Greenbelt, MD, Goddard Earth Sciences Data and Information Services Center (GES DISC), doi:10.5067/GPM/IMERG/3B-MONTH/07
source.licence: NASA open data (GES DISC data use guidelines)
processing: Downloaded only the precipitation field over a box around Bangladesh through NASA's OPeNDAP service (values unchanged).
Monthly rain = area-weighted mean rate (mm/hr) over the 0.1-degree cells whose centre lies inside the Bangladesh border (Natural Earth), times the hours in the month.
Monsoon rainfall = June + July + August + September total; only years with all four months.

describe.what: Total rain over Bangladesh in the monsoon months, June to September, from NASA's GPM satellites (IMERG).
describe.whyItMatters: The monsoon brings most of the year's rain: too much floods rivers and fields, too little harms the rice harvest.

notes: June-September total, averaged over the country, division or district.
Rain varies a lot from year to year, so a trend needs many years to detect.
Satellite estimate (GPM and TRMM radiometers, gauge-adjusted each month), averaged over the whole country; not the rain at any one station.
1998-2014 comes from the TRMM-era satellites and 2014 onward from GPM, processed together in version 07.
Monsoon rain swings a lot from year to year, so a trend needs many years to detect.
IMERG cells are about 11 km, so a small district averages only a handful of them.
Testing many divisions at once: about 1 test in 20 can look significant by chance alone, so check whether neighbouring divisions agree before trusting a single one.
Cross-check: NASA POWER (a weather-model product) shows a rising 1998-2025 monsoon trend that this satellite record does not; model rainfall trends can drift, so the satellite record is used here.

name: Submerged coastal land

source.name: JRC Global Surface Water, Yearly Water Classification History (Landsat)
source.citation: Pekel, J.-F., Cottam, A., Gorelick, N., Belward, A.S. (2016), High-resolution mapping of global surface water and its long-term changes, Nature 540, 418-422, doi:10.1038/nature20584. Source: EC JRC/Google.
source.licence: Free to use with attribution (Copernicus programme, EC JRC)
processing: Downloaded the two 10x10-degree yearly classification tiles that cover Bangladesh (80-100E, 20-30N) for every year 1988-2021 from the JRC open data server (values unchanged).
Baseline land: 30 m pixels seen in at least 2 of the years 1988-1992 (Landsat saw almost nothing of Bangladesh before 1988) and classed 'not water' in most of them.
Each year: total area (km2, true pixel area) of baseline-land pixels classed permanent water, inside the region's border (pixel centre inside).
A year is left empty when more than 10% of the region's baseline land had no clear Landsat view that year; nothing is filled in.

describe.what: How much land has turned into permanent water since the late 1980s, mapped from Landsat satellite images (JRC Global Surface Water).
describe.whyItMatters: Land lost to the sea and rivers means lost fields, homes and mangroves. Rising seas, erosion and sinking land all push the coast inland.

notes: Area (km2) that was land in 1988-1992 and is permanent water in that year, from Landsat images (30 m pixels).
Counts every cause of land turning to water: sea level rise, coastal and river-bank erosion, sinking land and new ponds or fish farms. It cannot separate sea level rise from the others.
Loss only: new land that forms (for example new islands in the Meghna estuary) is not subtracted.
Seasonal water (wet-season flooding) is not counted; only water present all year.
Years with too few clear Landsat images over the region are left empty (for example 1998).
Landsat 7 (1999) and Landsat 8 (2013) added more clear images; a year with more images can show slightly more permanent water, so small steps at those years are possible.

name: Ice mass from gravity (GRACE)

source.name: GRACE/GRACE-FO JPL mascons RL06.3Mv04 CRI (PO.DAAC)
source.citation: Wiese, D. N., Yuan, D.-N., Boening, C., Landerer, F. W., Watkins, M. M. (2023). JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO Mascon Ocean, Ice, and Hydrology Equivalent Water Height Coastal Resolution Improvement (CRI) Filtered JPL RL06.3Mv04. PO.DAAC. https://doi.org/10.5067/TEMSC-3JC634
source.licence: NASA open data (PO.DAAC data use and citation guidelines)
processing: Downloaded the global monthly mascon grid unchanged.

Mass change = sum over the 0.5-degree cells whose centre lies inside the region outline of water-equivalent thickness x cell area (1 cm of water on 1 m2 = 10 kg), in Gt, relative to the source's 2004.0-2009.999 mean.
1-sigma = the source's per-cell uncertainty summed within each ~300 km mascon and combined as independent errors between mascons.
Months with no solution (including the 2017-2018 mission gap) stay as gaps, never interpolated.

describe.what: Mass change of the ice in a region, weighed month by month by the GRACE and GRACE-FO satellites, which measure tiny changes in Earth's gravity.
describe.whyItMatters: The same method for Greenland, Antarctica and the Himalayas, so their losses can be compared directly; about 362 Gt of ice is 1 mm of global sea level.

notes: Relative to the 2004-2009 average.
GRACE sees about 300 km detail.
Measured by gravity: GRACE weighs all mass, so near the coast and in the Himalayas some of the signal is water or ocean mass, not ice.

Himalayas: the arc is about as wide as GRACE's resolution (~300 km); groundwater loss in the plains of northern India and Pakistan leaks into this signal, so treat the Himalayan trend as an upper bound on glacier loss.

Antarctica: GRACE totals depend strongly on the correction for land still rising after the last ice age (GIA); for 2002-2023 GRACE gives about -131 Gt/yr against IMBIE's reconciled -184 Gt/yr. Greenland agrees closely (about -249 against -253 Gt/yr).
A different method from the IMBIE ice mass record (which combines gravity, altimetry and input-output); the two are not independent but should agree closely for Greenland and Antarctica.
